\end{comment}
Turning to the bounds for $N^\theta_\mathsf{x}-N^\theta_\mathsf{y}$,  we have analogously to (\ref{f1.2}),  that
\begin{align}
N^\theta_{\mathsf{x}}-N^\theta_{\mathsf{y}}&=\sum_{i=1}^{\widetilde  N_{\bf 0}}( A^\theta_{\mathsf{x},i} -B^\theta_{\mathsf{y},i}),\label{f1.2-new}
\end{align}
for $A^{\theta}_{\mathsf{x},i}$ and $B^\theta_{\mathsf{y},i}$ of (\ref{angle.12}).  Reducing $\delta_o$ as needed,  
the same reasoning yields the bounds (\ref{height.70a}) 
and (\ref{height.74a}) with $N_\mathsf{x}^\theta-N_\mathsf{y}^\theta$ instead of $N_\mathsf{x}-N_\mathsf{y}$ 
(note that we made sure to have $e^{-\frac{\bar n_\varepsilon}{2}} n_\varepsilon \to 0$ and 
$\sqrt{\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})} \lambda^2 n_\varepsilon^2$ uniformly bounded).
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
By the Cramer-Wold device,  it suffices for \Cref{theo-mclt} to fix 
$\{\mathsf{x}_i,  i \le p\}$,  $\{\lambda_i,  i \le 2p\} \in \mathbb{R}^{2p}$ and prove the {\sc\lowercase{clt}}-s for 
\[
\mathcal{O}^{(\varepsilon)}_{\rm in} :=
\sum_{i=1}^{2p} \lambda_i q^{(\varepsilon)}_{\rm in} (i) \quad {\rm and} \quad 
\mathcal{O}^{(\varepsilon)}_{\rm out}:=
\sum_{i=1}^{2p} \lambda_i q^{(\varepsilon)}_{\rm out} (i) \,.
\]
To this end,  note that conditionally on $\mathcal{H}_{\mathsf{k}_\varepsilon(z)}$ the $\mathbb{R}$-valued $\mathcal{O}^{(\varepsilon)}_{\rm in}$ is of the form
\begin{equation}\label{def:O-vep-in}
\mathcal{O}^{(\varepsilon)}_{\rm in} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathsf{k}_\varepsilon(z)}} \sum_{j=1}^{\mathsf{k}_\varepsilon(z)}
\big(  \mathcal{O}_j  - \mathbb{E}[ \mathcal{O} |\mathsf{z}_{(j-1)2},\mathsf{z}_{j1}] \big)  \,,
\end{equation}
where the conditionally independent $\mathcal{O}_j \overset{\rm dist}{=} \mathcal{O}(\mathsf{z},\mathsf{z}')$ count the contribution 
to $\mathcal{O}^{(\varepsilon)}_{\rm in}$ between the $(j-1)$'st and $j$'th inter-city excursions,  starting at $\mathsf{z} \in \partial \mathbb{C}$ and 
ending at $\mathsf{z}' \in \partial \mathbb{C}^\mathsf{e}$.  Indeed,  with $\sqrt{\mathsf{k}_\varepsilon(z)}=\mathsf{a} (\mathsf{m}_\varepsilon+z)$,
$\mathsf{a}:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \mathsf{t}_1}}$,  we have 
\begin{equation}\label{def:OO-z}
\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{z},\mathsf{z}')  \overset{\rm dist}{=}
\sum_{i=1}^p \sum_{\ell=1}^{T_{\mathsf{x}_i,\mathsf {K}_{1}}^{\partial \mathbb{C}^\mathsf{e}(1)}}
\psi_i(\theta_{\ell,\mathsf{x}_i})\,,
\end{equation}
aggregating during such single inter-city excursion,  over all $\mathsf {K}_{1}$-level excursions of $\{\mathsf{x}_i,  i \le p \}$ 
with angle increments $\{\theta_{\ell,\mathsf{x}_i}\}$,  the uniformly bounded scores 
\[
\psi_{i}(\theta):=\mathsf{a} \Big\{\lambda_i + \lambda_{i+p}  \bar c[\langle \cos(\cdot),\bar \mu \rangle - \cos (\theta)]\Big\}\,.
\]
The uniform separation between $\bigcup \{ \mathbb{B}_{\mathsf{d}} (\mathsf{v}, r_{\mathsf {K}_{1}}) :  \mathsf{v} \in \mathbb{A}_u^o,  u \le \mathsf {M} \}$,
$\partial \mathbb{C}$ and $\partial \mathbb{C}^{\mathsf{e}}$ implies a uniform fourth moment control  
\[
\sup_{\mathsf{z},\mathsf{z}',\mathsf{v}} \mathbb{E} \Big[\big(T_{\mathsf{v},\mathsf {K}_{1}}^{\partial \mathbb{C}^\mathsf{e}(1)}\big)^4\, \big|\,  \mathsf{z},\mathsf{z}' \Big] < \infty \,,
\]
and thereby the same uniform control on $\sup_{\mathsf{z},\mathsf{z}'} \mathbb{E} [\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{z},\mathsf{z}')^4]$.  We thus deduce by
Lyapunov's {\sc\lowercase{clt}},  that as $\varepsilon \to 0$,  the variables $\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\mathsf{k}_\varepsilon(z)}^{-1} \mathcal{O}^{(\varepsilon)}_{\rm in}$ converge
in law conditionally on $\mathcal{H}_{\mathsf{k}_\varepsilon(z)}$,  to a standard normal,  where 
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma}_k^2 := \frac{1}{k} \sum_{j=1}^{k} f(\mathsf{z}_{(j-1)2},\mathsf{z}_{j1}) \quad {\rm for} \quad 
f(\mathsf{z},\mathsf{z}') := {\sf var}\big(\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{z},\mathsf{z}')|\mathsf{z},\mathsf{z}'\big) \,.
\] 
Our fourth moment control implies that $f(\cdot,\cdot)$ is uniformly bounded.  Thus,  when $k \to \infty$, 
a.s.  $\boldsymbol{\sigma}_k^2 \to \langle f,  \bar \mu_\mathsf{e} \rangle$ by the {\sc\lowercase{lln}} for integrable functions of such 
Doeblin chains (see \cite[Theorem 17.0.1]{Meyn-Tweedie}).  Replacing the random $\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\mathsf{k}_\varepsilon(z)}$
by the non-random $\sqrt{\langle f,  \bar \mu_\mathsf{e} \rangle}$ thus concludes the proof of the conditional 
{\sc\lowercase{clt}} for $\mathcal{O}^{(\varepsilon)}_{\rm in}$ and consequently,  of (\ref{mCLT.03}).
Next,  note that similarly to (\ref{def:O-vep-in}),   
\begin{equation}\label{def:O-vep-out}
\mathcal{O}^{(\varepsilon)}_{\rm out} = \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_{\mathsf{k}_\varepsilon(z)} \quad {\rm for} \quad 
\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_k := \frac{1}{\sqrt{k}} \sum_{j=1}^{k}
\big(  \mathbb{E}[ \mathcal{O} |\mathsf{z}_{(j-1)2},\mathsf{z}_{j1}] - \mathbb{E}_{\bar \mu_\mathsf{e}} [\mathcal{O}] \big)  \,.
\end{equation}
As $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{z},\mathsf{z}')$ of (\ref{def:OO-z}) have uniformly bounded moments,  
                                   
$\mathbb{E}[ \mathcal{O} |\mathsf{z},\mathsf{z}'] - \mathbb{E}_{\bar \mu_\mathsf{e}} [\mathcal{O}]$ is uniformly bounded,  
of zero $\bar \mu_\mathsf{e}$-mean.  Consequently,  $\{\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_k\}$ satisfies the {\sc\lowercase{clt}} (see 
\cite[Theorem 17.0.1]{Meyn-Tweedie}),  with some finite variance 
(of a form analogous to (\ref{eq:var-erg})).  In particular,  having established the {\sc\lowercase{CLT}}
for $\mathcal{O}^{(\varepsilon)}_{\rm out}$ yields (\ref{mCLT.04}),  thereby completing the proof 
of the proposition.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
The tower property of conditional expectations allows us to
replace the stated expectations under the invariant law $\bar \mu_{\mathsf{e}}$ on $\partial \mathbb{C} \times \partial \mathbb{C}^\mathsf{e}$
by such expectations with respect to (only) the invariant law $\mu_\mathsf{e}$ on $\partial \mathbb{C}$.  Having done so, 
for (\ref{17.02b}) set $R=r_{\mathsf {K}_{1}-1}$,  $r=r_{\mathsf {K}_{1}}$ and denote by $D_1$ the time  
to go from $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d} (\mathsf{x},R)$ to  $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d} (\mathsf{x},r)$ and back to $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},R)$.
Recall \cite[Lemma 8.1]{BK} that 
starting at the unique invariant measure $\mu_{\mathsf{x},r}^R$ for such $\mathsf {K}_{1}$-level excursions,  yields
$\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\mathsf{x},r}^R}[D_1] =\frac{1}{\pi}$.
Further,  by an ergodic consideration (similar to the argument used in proving \Cref{lem-equalmean}),  it takes
$\frac{(k+o(k)) \mathsf{t}_1}{\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\mathsf{e}}} \big[T_{\mathsf{x},\mathsf {K}_{1}}^{\partial \mathbb{C}^\mathsf{e}(1)} \big]}$ time till 
completing the $k$-th $\mathsf {K}_{1}$-level excursion around $\mathsf{x}$,  which on the other hand 
must also take $(k+o(k)) \mathbb{E}_{\mu_{\mathsf{x},r}^R}[D_1]$ time.  Equating the leading 
orders of both expressions yields (\ref{17.02b}).  Further,  recall that $\bar \mu$ 
of the paragraph containing (\ref{dfn:Poiss}),  is the invariant law of the angle-differences $\{\theta_{j,\mathsf{x}}\}$.  As it
must match the law induced on these angle-differences
by starting at the invariant measure $\mu_\mathsf{e}$ on $\partial \mathbb{C}$,  we get (\ref{17.02c}) out of (\ref{17.02b}).
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
\label{prop:coupling} 
For some universal $\bar c>1$,
                 
any $\kappa>0$ small enough, integer $m' \in [m+a,m+b]$, 
$b-a \le \frac{\sqrt{m}}{\kappa}$ and $(m,k,r,b) \in \Theta_\kappa$ of
(\ref{dfn:Thetak}), there exists a coupling, possibly depending on $m',m,a,b,k,r,R$,
of the two collections of inner excursions
distributed according to $\mathbb{P}_{m,a,b}$ and $\mathbb{P}^\star_{m'}$,
where the $\Delta_{m,a,b}$ different inner excursions are such that 
\begin{align}\label{eq:coupling}
\sup_{\Theta_\kappa,a,m'} \, \Big\{ \frac{e^r}{k} \mathbb{P} \big( \Delta_{m,a,b} \ge 7  r {\bar c} \kappa \sqrt{m} \big) \Big\} < \infty \,.
\end{align}
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- remark-20: body_md -->
\label{rmk:a-eq-b}
We prove Proposition \ref{prop:coupling} only for $a=b$ (and $m'=m+b$), adopting 
the notations $\mathcal{A}_{m,b}$, $\mathbb{P}_{m,b}$ and $\Delta_{m,b}$, for $\mathcal{A}^{(k)}_{m,b,b}$
$\mathbb{P}_{m,b,b}$ and $\Delta_{m,b,b}$, respectively. Indeed, 
since (\ref{eq:coupling}) trivially holds for $r \le r_o$ and any $r_o(\kappa)$ finite,  we may replace
the stated constraint on $b-a$ by $b-a \le r \kappa \sqrt{m}$. Further,  
$\mathbb{P}_{m,a,b}$ is a mixture of the laws $\mathbb{P}_{m,u}$, $u \in [a,b]$ and  
the number of different excursions between $\mathbb{P}^\star_{m_1}$ and $\mathbb{P}^\star_{m_2}$ is at most
$|m_1-m_2|$. It follows that weighting the coupling between $\mathbb{P}_{m,u}$ and $\mathbb{P}^\star_{m+u}$ 
as in Proposition \ref{prop:coupling}, according to these mixture coefficients, increases the 
number of different excursions with respect to $\mathbb{P}^\star_{m'}$, for any fixed $m' \in [m+a,m+b]$,
by at most $b-a \le r \kappa \sqrt{m}$. Thus, multiplying $\bar c$ by $8/7$ yields the general case, as stated.
<!-- end remark-20 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Setting hereafter $a=b$, $m'=m+b$,
we simplify the task of proving Proposition \ref{prop:coupling} upon noting that 
our inner Brownian excursions are independent conditional 
on the pairs $\mathsf{y}=(\mathsf{y}^{(1)},\mathsf{y}^{(2)})$, where
$\mathsf{y}^{(1)} \in \partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},R e^{-k})$  
and $\mathsf{y}^{(2)} \in \partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},R e^{-(k-1)})$ denote 
the starting and ending positions, respectively, of each excursion, 
        
with the conditional law of each such inner excursion determined by the value of the corresponding 
pair $\mathsf{y}$. It thus suffices to provide a coupling between the joint laws $\mathbb{P}_{m,b}$ and $\mathbb{P}^\star_{m'}$ 
of the corresponding two collections $\{\mathsf{y}_{i} \}$, such that
the bound (\ref{eq:coupling}) applies for the number $\Delta_{m,b}$ 
of differences between these two un-ordered lists. To this end, note that  
the consecutive starting and ending positions $\mathsf{y}^{(o)}_i=(\mathsf{y}_i^{(o,1)},\mathsf{y}_i^{(o,2)})$
of the outer excursions, form a Markov chain, whose transition probabilities are composed 
of the outer part, yielding the conditional law of $\mathsf{y}_{i}^{(o,1)} \in  \partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},R)$
given $\mathsf{y}_{i-1}^{(o,2)} \in \partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0}, e R)$ and the inner 
part, namely the conditional law of $\mathsf{y}_i^{(o,2)}$ given $\mathsf{y}_i^{(o,1)}$. By
the same reasoning as in the proof of  Lemma \ref{lem:conc},
                                                                                    
                   
the conditional law of $\mathsf{y}_i^{(o,1)}$ given $\mathsf{y}_{i-1}^{(o,2)}$ 
has a uniformly in $R \le e^{-2}$, bounded away from zero density {\sc\lowercase{wrt}} 
Lebesgue's measure on the corresponding circle. The Markov chain $\{\mathsf{y}_i^{(o)}\}$
is thus Doeblin aperiodic (satisfying 
           
\cite[(16.9)]{Meyn-Tweedie}), admitting infinitely many renewal times $\{T_j, j \ge 1\}$,
where $\mathsf{y}^{(o,1)}$ is uniformly distributed, independently of the past,  
with {\sc\lowercase{iid}} positive Geometric ($1/c'$) inter-renewal distances 
\[
\chi_j := T_{j+1} - T_j,  \qquad \forall j \ge 0, 
\]
for some universal $c'>1$ (where $T_0=0$, so $\chi_0=T_1$).
                                                                      

Further, fixing $k \ge 1$, the unconditioned counts $\{L^{(k)}_i, i \ge 1\}$ of inner excursions completed 
during the consecutive outer excursions,
                                                                                               
           
                                                                                                 
                                                                                     
                        
are {\sc\lowercase{iid}} and independent 
of the sequence $\{\chi_j\}_{j \ge 0}$.
                                                                                        
                                              
                                                      
                                                                     
                                           
                       
                                                                             
                            
For any $j \ge 0$, there are
\[
 \bar L^{(k)}_j := \sum_{i=0}^{\chi_j-1} L_{T_j+i}^{(k)}
\]
inner excursions between the $j$-th and $(j+1)$-st renewal events, to which correspond under $\mathbb{P}^\star$ 
the mutually independent segments $\bar \mathcal{Y}_j^{(k)} := \{\mathsf{y}_i : i \in [T_j,T_{j+1})\}$
between the consecutive renewal events. Per $k \ge 1$,
                                                                 
the law of each $\bar \mathcal{Y}_j^{(k)}$, $j \ne 0$, depends only on the value of 
$\mathcal{L}^{(k)}_j := \{\chi_j, L_{T_j+i}^{(k)}, i\in [0,\chi_j)\}$. Thus, we first construct 
the blocks $\mathcal{L}^{(k)}_j$ out of  the
independent {\sc\lowercase{iid}} $\{L^{(k)}_i, i \ge 1\}$ and $\{\chi_j, j \ge 0\}$. Thereafter,
given these blocks
              
we construct the conditionally independent segments $\bar \mathcal{Y}^{(k)}_j$.
                                        
During the first $\ell$ outer excursions there are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:M-ell-def}
M_\ell := \sup \{ j \ge 0 : T_j \le \ell \} 
\end{equation}
renewal events, and we note that for any fixed $j \in [1,M_m)$, the law of $\bar \mathcal{Y}_j^{(k)}$ is 
affected by conditioning on $\mathcal{A}_{m,b}$ only via the change 
in the law of $\mathcal{L}^{(k)}_j$.

The measure $\mathbb{P}_{m,b}$ on the collection $\{\mathsf{y}_i\}$ is then induced by the  
law $\mathbb{Q}_{m,b}$ of $\{\widetilde{L}_i, i \le m\}$, namely the {\sc\lowercase{iid}} $\{L_i=L^{(k)}_i, i \le m\}$ 
conditional on the event $\mathcal{A}_{m,b}=\mathcal{A}^{(k)}_{m,b,b}$ 
of (\ref{eq:Amb-def}) (and hereafter we often suppress the index $k$ in order to lessen the notations). 
The stopping time $\tau_h$ of (\ref{def:tau-h}) counts for such $L^{(k)}$
the number of outer excursions up to the completion of $h$ inner excursions, 
and the measure $\mathbb{P}^\star_{m'}$ on the unconditional $\{\mathsf{y}_i, i \le m'\}$ is thus likewise
induced by the law
$\mathbb{Q}^\star_{m'}$ of \Cref{lem:coupling}.
                                           
                                        
                                                                
                            
                                        
                                                                          
               

In view of the preceding discussion we note that for any given matched
block $\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_j=\mathcal{L}^\star_j$,  we can and shall construct \emph{the same Brownian 
path between the corresponding pairs of renewal events} in our two sequences, 
thereby matching the relevant (ordered) segments $\bar \mathcal{Y}$ of the $\mathsf{y}_i$ values. Turning 
to construct (couple) the values of $\mathsf{y}_i$ in the collection $\bar \mathcal{U}_{m,b}$ of 
non-matched blocks of outer excursions, note that by definition, $\bar \mathcal{U}_{m,b}$ induces
a collection $\mathcal{U}_{m,b}$ of 
$\bar \Delta_{m,b}$ positive summands $\{\widetilde{L}_{(\alpha)}, L^\star_{(\alpha^\star)}\}$, such that 
due to our choice of $m'=m+b$,
\[
\sum_\alpha \widetilde{L}_{(\alpha)} = \sum_{\alpha^\star} L^\star_{(\alpha^\star)} 
\]
(compare (\ref{eq:Amb-def}) for $a=b$, with (\ref{eq:Amb-star-def})). 
We then further partition the positive integer entries of $\mathcal{U}_{m,b}$ to yield, 
after re-ordering, at most $\bar \Delta_{m,b}$ parts satisfying 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:unmatch-piece}
\widehat{L}_{(\alpha)}=\widehat{L}^\star_{(\alpha^\star)} \ge 1 \,.
\end{equation}
Indeed, taking initially $\widehat{L}_{(\alpha)}=\widetilde{L}_{(\alpha)}$ and $\widehat{L}^\star_{(\alpha^\star)}=
L^\star_{(\alpha^\star)}$, we iteratively pair the $\arg\min_\alpha \{ \widehat{L}_{(\alpha)} \}$ with 
$\arg\min_{\alpha^\star} \{ \widehat{L}^\star_{(\alpha^\star)} \}$,
removing from consideration the common (matched) parts, after cutting as needed 
the larger of these two length.
With each step reducing the total number of yet unmatched parts of elements from $\mathcal{U}_{m,b}$, 
we have the stated complete matching after at most $\bar \Delta_{m,b}$ operations. 
Now, let $R e^{-k} e^{i \mathsf{z}_j}$, 
for $0 \le j \le \ell$ denote the starting positions of the $\ell$ inner excursions 
which form such generic piece of an outer excursion, say $(\alpha)$, 
consisting of $\widehat{L}_{(\alpha)}=\ell$ inner excursions, with 
$R e^{-k} e^{i \mathsf{z}^\star_j}$ for the starting positions in the corresponding paired
piece $(\alpha^\star)$ of some outer excursion in our other sequence. Conditional on the totality of 
$\{\widetilde{L}_i,L^\star_i,\chi_j\}$ and in particular on the identity and length of  
all matched parts appearing in (\ref{eq:unmatch-piece}),  by radial symmetry of the 
Brownian motion within $\mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},e R)$, the collections $\{ \mathsf{z}_{j} - \mathsf{z}_{j-1}, 1 \le j \le \ell \}$
and $\{\mathsf{z}^\star_j-\mathsf{z}^\star_{j-1}, 1 \le j \le \ell \}$, are each composed of 
{\sc\lowercase{iid}} $[2 \pi]$-valued variables, of density which is uniformly over $k \ge 1$ and $R \le e^{-2}$, bounded
below by some $1/c'' > 0$. Thus, even after the (paired) collection 
$\{\widehat{L}_{(\alpha)}, \widehat{L}^\star_{(\alpha^\star)} \}$ is specified, there exist {\sc\lowercase{IID}} Bernoulli($1/c''$) 
variables associated with the starting positions $\mathsf{y}_i^{(1)}$ of the unmatched inner excursions 
corresponding to $\mathcal{U}_{m,b}$, 
                           
except the first one in each piece,
                              
whose occurrence signify the renewal event whereby the current 
$\mathsf{y}^{(1)}_i$ will be chosen uniformly, independently of the past. The corresponding 
distances $\widehat{\chi}_{(\alpha)}$ and $\widehat{\chi}^\star_{(\alpha^\star)}$ from
the start of a generic piece $(\alpha)$ or $(\alpha^\star)$, respectively, till the 
first such renewal, are {\sc\lowercase{iid}} positive Geometric($1/c''$). Further, after all such 
$\{\widehat{\chi}_{(\alpha)}, \widehat{\chi}^\star_{(\alpha^\star)}\}$ are chosen, the 
Brownian segments within the different unmatched pieces of both sequences, 
starting at the first renewal event in each piece, are independent of each other, with 
the law of any such segment determined solely by the remaining length within that 
piece, namely by $\widehat{L}_{(\alpha)}-\widehat{\chi}_{(\alpha)}$ and  
$\widehat{L}^\star_{(\alpha^\star)}-\widehat{\chi}^\star_{(\alpha^\star)}$, respectively. It thus follows
that the coupling $\widehat{\chi}_{(\alpha)}=\widehat{\chi}^\star_{(\alpha^\star)}$ for each pair
$(\alpha)$ and $(\alpha^\star)$ of (\ref{eq:unmatch-piece}), allows one  
to use the same Brownian path for each such pair, except for at most 
the first $\widehat{\chi}_{(\alpha)}$ inner excursions within that piece. Thereby we arrive at 
          
\[
\Delta_{m,b} \le \sum_{(\alpha)} \widehat{\chi}_{(\alpha)} \,,
\]
where the sum is over at most $\bar \Delta_{m,b}$ indices $(\alpha)$, conditional on which 
the variables $\{ \widehat{\chi}_{(\alpha)} \}$ remain {\sc\lowercase{iid}} Geometric($1/c''$). 
In conclusion,  the bound of 
Lemma \ref{lem:coupling} on $\bar \Delta_{m,b}$, together with standard exponential tails for
sum of {\sc\lowercase{iid}} Geometric variables, complete the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:coupling}.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- lemma-39: body_md -->
\label{lem:HigherMomentBound}
Denote by $\mathbb{E}^{\mathsf{z},\mathsf{v}}(\cdot)$ the expectation over the excursion $\widetilde{X}^1$ which 
starts at $\mathsf{z} \in\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},\tilde{r})$,  conditional on ending at 
$\mathsf{v} \in \partial \mathbb{B}_{\mathsf{d}}({\bf 0},\tilde{R})$.  
For some $q_{1}=q_{1}(a,b)<\frac{1}{2}$,   
$c_3=c_3(a,b)<\infty$ and any $\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y} \in \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d} ({\bf 0},\tilde{r}-R)$ with $q:=\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})/R \leq q_{1}$,
if $\lambda>0$ and $e^{4 \pi \lambda} < 1/(q c_3)$,  then 
\begin{equation}
\label{eq-zav1}
 \sup_{\mathsf{z},\mathsf{v}} \mathbb{E}^{\mathsf{z},\mathsf{v}} \Big( \exp(\lambda |A_{\mathsf{x},1}-B_{\mathsf{y},1}|) \Big) \leq 
 \exp\big (c_3 q (e^{4 \pi \lambda}-1)\big) \,.
\end{equation} 
With $q=\sqrt{\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})/R}$,  the same bound applies for $|A^\theta_{\mathsf{x},1}-B^\theta_{\mathsf{y},1}|$.
<!-- end lemma-39 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
Fixing $\mathsf{x}$ and $\mathsf{y}$,  consider the following subsets of $\mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},\tilde{r})$:
\begin{align*}
\Gamma_1& := \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},r)\cap \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{y},r)\,,\quad\;
\Gamma_2:= \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},r)\cup \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{y}, r)\,, \\
\Gamma_3&:= \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},R)\cap \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{y},R)\,,\quad
\Gamma_4:= \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},R)\cup \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{y},R)\,,
\end{align*}
 \begin{figure}[h]
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}
\draw[red] (-.1,0) circle(1.5);
\draw[red]  (-.1,0) circle(3);
  \fill (-.1,0) circle (1pt) [red] node[red, left] {${\mathsf{x}}$};
   \fill (-1.5,0)  node[blue, right] {$\Gamma_1$};
    \fill (-2.4,0)  node[green, right] {$\partial \Gamma_2$};
     \fill (-3.9,0)  node[purple, right] {$\partial \Gamma_4$};
      \fill (-3,0)  node[orange, right] {$\Gamma_3$};
  \draw (.1,0) circle(1.5);
\draw (.1,0) circle(3);
  \fill (.1,0) circle (1pt) node[right] {$\mathsf{y}$};
   \fill (0.8,0)  node[blue, right] {$\Gamma_1$};
    \fill (1.5,0)  node[green, right] {$\partial \Gamma_2$};
     \fill (2.3,0)  node[orange, right] {$\Gamma_3$};
      \fill (3,0)  node[purple, right] {$\partial \Gamma_4$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
\caption{\small Boundary of $\textcolor{blue}{\Gamma_1},  \textcolor{green}{\Gamma_2}, 
\textcolor{orange}{\Gamma_3} ,  \textcolor{purple}{\Gamma_4}$ 
($R=2r$,  $q=\frac{1}{15}$,  {$\mathsf{x}$-balls in red}).}
\label{angle1}
\end{figure}
noting that $q_1<(1-b)/2$ guarantees that $\Gamma_2 \subseteq \Gamma_3$ (see Figure \ref{angle1}). 
Thus we have that 
\[
\Gamma_1 \subset \Gamma_2 \subset \Gamma_3 \subset \Gamma_4  \,.
\]
In addition to the
                   
$\mathsf{x}$-excursions from $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},r)$ to $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},R)$ 
and the 
                     
$\mathsf{y}$-excursions from $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{y},r)$ to $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{y},R)$ 
within our excursion around ${\bf 0}$,  we consider also the consecutive \emph{$(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})$-excursions} defined
to be the excursions of the Brownian path from $\partial \Gamma_2$ to $\partial \Gamma_4$,   and note that each 
$(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})$-excursion must contain at least one $\mathsf{x}$ or $\mathsf{y}$-excursion (see also Figure \ref{angle1}).
We call an $(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})$-excursion \emph{special} if the path enters $\partial \Gamma_1$ before $\partial \Gamma_3$ and do not visit $\Gamma_2$ after entering $\partial \Gamma_3$.   Note the following elementary relations:\\
$\bullet$ Any $\mathsf{x}$-excursion contains a path from $\partial \Gamma_2$ 
to $\partial \Gamma_3$;\\
$\bullet$ Any $\mathsf{y}$-excursion contains a path from $\partial \Gamma_2$ to $\partial \Gamma_3$;\\
$\bullet$ A path from $\partial \Gamma_1$ to $\partial \Gamma_4$ contains 
       
an  
$\mathsf{x}$-excursion and  $\mathsf{y}$-excursion;\\
$\bullet$ In a special $(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})$-excursion lies exactly one $\mathsf{x}$-excursion and 
one $\mathsf{y}$-excursion. \\ 

If the $j$-th $(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})$-excursion is special,  set $C_j:=0$ 
and $C^\theta_j:=|\cos(\theta)-\cos(\theta')|$ for the angle-differences $\theta$ and $\theta'$ of the $\mathsf{x}$ and $\mathsf{y}$ 
excursions inside this $(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})$-excursion.  If the $j$-th $(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})$-excursion is non-special, 
set  $C^\theta_j:=0$ and $C_j \ge 1$ be the number of excursions from $\partial \Gamma_2$ 
to $\partial \Gamma_3$ during this non-special $(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})$-excursion.  It is then easy to verify that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:geo-bd-ad}
|A_{\mathsf{x},1}-B_{\mathsf{y},1}| \le 2 \sum_j C_j \,,  \qquad |A^\theta_{\mathsf{x},1}-B^\theta_{\mathsf{y},1}| \le \sum_j (2 C_j + C^\theta_j)  \,.
\end{equation}
Let $\mathsf {G}^o_p$ denote a \emph{non-negative} Geometric($1-p$) variable (so $\mathbb{P}(\mathsf {G}^o_{p} \ge k)=  p^k$ for $k \ge 0$) 
and $\mathcal{B}_p$ a Bernoulli($p$) variable independent of it.  We proceed to show that for some 
$q_1(a,b)>0$,  $c=c(a,b)<\infty$ and all $q=\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})/R \le q_1$,  conditionally on the 
path up to the start of its $j$-th $(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})$-excursion,  we have the stochastic domination
\begin{align}\label{eq:st-dom}
C_j & \stackrel{\rm st}{\preccurlyeq} 2 \mathsf {G}^o_{cq}\,,  \\ 
\label{eq:st-dom-th}
2 C_j + C^\theta_j & \stackrel{\rm st}{\preccurlyeq} 4 \mathsf {G}^o_{cq} + c \sqrt{q} + 4 \pi \mathcal{B}_{c \sqrt{q}} \,.
\end{align}
To this end,  set $\mathsf{w}:=\frac{1}{2}(\mathsf{x}+\mathsf{y})$ and balls 
$\Gamma^\star_\ell:= \mathbb{B}_{\mathsf{d}}(\mathsf{w},\rho_\ell)$,  of radii 
\[
\rho_1:= r-\frac{1}{2} q R,  \quad \rho_2= r+\frac{1}{2}qR,  \quad \rho_3= R-\frac{1}{2}qR,  \quad \rho_4 = R+\frac{1}{2}qR \,.
\]
As $\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})=qR$,  it follows that 
\[
\Gamma^\star_1 \subset \Gamma_1 \subset \Gamma_2 \subset \Gamma^\star_2 \subset \Gamma^\star_3
\subset \Gamma_3 \subset \Gamma_4 \subset \Gamma^\star_4 \,.
\]
                                                            
                                                          
With
$\{C_j=1\}$ requiring that the $(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})$-excursion enter $\partial \Gamma_3$ before $\partial \Gamma_1$,
for any $\mathsf{u} \in \partial \Gamma_2$ we bound $\mathbb{P}^\mathsf{u}(C_j=1)$ by the maximum over starting points in $\partial \Gamma_2^\star$ of the 
           
probability of entering $\partial \Gamma_3^\star$ before $\partial \Gamma^\star_1$,  which is 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Cj-not-zero}
\gamma_1 := \frac{\log\Big(\frac{2 r+qR}{2r-qR}\Big)}{\log\Big(\frac{2R-qR}{2r-qR}\Big)} \,.
\end{equation}
Likewise,  the event $\{C_j \ge k\}$ requires at least $k-1 \ge 1$ returns 
from $\partial \Gamma_3$ to $\partial \Gamma_2$ prior to hitting $\partial \Gamma_4$.
Starting anywhere on $\partial \Gamma_3$ the probability of hitting $\partial \Gamma_2$ 
prior to $\partial \Gamma_4$ is at most the maximum over starting points in $\partial \Gamma_3^\star$ 
of the 
          
probability of entering $\partial \Gamma^\star_2$ prior to 
$\partial \Gamma^\star_4$,  which is 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Cj-above-one}
\gamma_2:= \frac{\log\Big(\frac{2 R+qR}{2R-qR}\Big)}{\log\Big(\frac{2R+qR}{2r+qR}\Big)} \,.
\end{equation}
Clearly $\gamma_1 + \gamma_2 \le c q$ for any $q=\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})/R \le q_1<a$ and 
some $c=c(a,b,q_1)$ finite such that 
                                                
$c(a,b,q_1) q_1 \to 0$ when $q_1 \to 0$.  Assuming {\sc\lowercase{wlog}} that $c q_1 < 1$
and utilizing the strong Markov property of the Brownian path,  we thus arrive 
at $\mathbb{P}(C_j \ge k) \le (cq)^{k-{\bf 1}_{k \ge 2}}$.  To get  (\ref{eq:st-dom}) simply note
that $k-1 \ge k/2$ for $k \ge 2$.

Turning to (\ref{eq:st-dom-th}),  recall that for any special $(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})$-excursion, 
$\theta=\theta_{ +}-\theta_{-}$ where $\theta_{-}$ the angle at which it first hits $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},r)$ 
and $\theta_{+}$ the angle 
at which it first hits $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},R)$,  while analogously $\theta'=\theta'_{+}-\theta'_{-}$ for 
the inner $\mathsf{y}$-excursion,  so with $\|\cos(\cdot)\|_{\rm Lip} \le 1$,  clearly 
\[
C^\theta_j \le (|\theta'_{-}-\theta_{-}| + |\theta'_+ - \theta_+|) {\bf 1}_{\big\{\hbox{excursion}\; j \; \hbox{is special}\big\}} \,.
\]
                                                                
Focusing first on $|\theta_{-}-\theta'_{-}|$,  we assume {\sc\lowercase{wlog}} that our special $(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})$-excursion 
starts at $\mathsf{u} \in \partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},r)$ and construct a Cartesian coordinate system such that 
one axis contains the segment connecting $\mathsf{u}$ to $\mathsf{y}$ and the origin lies in $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{y},r)$,  
see Figure \ref{angle},  with $\mathsf{u}$ represented 
                                            
as $(0, u)$ for some $0<u \le qR$ and $\mathsf{y}=(0, -r)$.  Note that
      
$\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{y},r)$ 
                                                                   
intersects the line $L$ of height $-u$ at $(\pm z  ,-u)$ for $z:=\sqrt{r^2-(r-u)^2}$.
 \begin{figure}[h]
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}
\draw (0,-2) circle(2);
\draw (0,-4.5) -- (0,1.3);
\draw (-2,0) -- (2,0);
  \fill (0,-2) circle (2pt) node[right] {$\mathsf{y}=(0,-r)$};
  \fill (0,.5) circle (2pt) node[right] {$\mathsf{u}=(0,u)$};
  \fill (1.33,-.5) circle (2pt) node[below] {$\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\! (z,-u)$};
  \fill (-1.33,-.5) circle (2pt) node[below] {$\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; (-z,-u)$};
\draw (-3,-.5) -- (3,-.5);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
\caption{\small First hitting point}
\label{angle}
\end{figure}
Further measuring {\sc\lowercase{wlog}} the angles $\theta_-$ and $\theta'_{-}$ from $\mathsf{y}=(0, -r)$ we have that $\theta_{-}=0$ 
with $\theta'_{-}$ the angle from $(0,-r)$ of the point where the Brownian path,  started at $(0, u)$,  
first hits $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}\left(\mathsf{y},r\right)$.  Denote by $\tau$ the first hitting time 
of $L$ by a Brownian path $(X_t,  t \ge 0)$ started at $X_0=(0, u)$, 
with $X_{\tau}:=(x_{\tau}, -u)$.  Because we deal with a special excursion,  necessarily $\tau$ is smaller
than the hitting time of $\partial \Gamma_3$.  Note that if 
$|x_{\tau}|< z$ then the Brownian path $X_t$ must first hits $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{y},r)$ 
on the upper arc of $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{y},r)$ between $(z,-u)$ and $(-z,-u)$.  In that case 
$|\theta'_{-}|$ is at most the angle of the point $(z,-u)$ measured from $\mathsf{y}=(0, -r)$.  That is, 
\[
|\theta'_{-}| \le \tan^{ -1}\Big(\frac{z}{r-u}\Big) \le \tan^{-1} \Big(\sqrt{(1-qR/r)^{-2}-1}\Big) \le \frac{c}{2} \sqrt{q} \,,
\]
for some $c=c(a,q_1)<\infty$ and any $q \le q_1$.   
Consequently,  
\[
|\theta'_{-}-\theta_-| 
                                               
                                                                              
          
\leq \frac{c}{2} \sqrt{q} + 2\pi {\bf 1}_{\{   |x_{\tau}|\geq z\}}.
\]
    
      
 Further,  by the Poisson kernel for the upper half-plane
 \begin{align*}
 \mathbb{P}^{ \(   0,u \)} ( |x_{\tau}|\geq z ) 
                                                         
 =  \frac{2}{\pi}\int_{z/(2u)}^{ \infty} \frac{1}{s^2+1}\,ds
                                                                  
  &= \frac{2}{\pi} \tan^{-1} \Big(\frac{2u}{z}\Big) \nonumber \\
  &\le \frac{2}{\pi} \tan^{-1} \Big(\frac{2\sqrt{qR}}{\sqrt{2r-qR}}\Big)
\leq \frac{c}{2} \sqrt{q},  \nonumber
 \end{align*}
for any $q \le q_1$ and some $c=c(a,q_1) < \infty$ such that $c \sqrt{q_1} <1$.  
Omitting the similar analysis for $|\theta_+-\theta'_{+}|$,  we conclude that 
conditionally of the path up to the start of its $j$-th $(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})$-excursion,  the 
variable $C^\theta_j$ is stochastically dominated by $c\sqrt{q}+4 \pi \mathcal{B}_{c\sqrt{q}}$.  
Further,  $C^\theta_j>0$ only for special excursions,  whereby $C_j=0$,  allowing us to take 
$\mathcal{B}_{c \sqrt{q}}$ independent of $\mathsf {G}^o_{cq}$ in (\ref{eq:st-dom-th}).


Having proved (\ref{eq:st-dom}) and (\ref{eq:st-dom-th}) for each $(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})$-excursion,  
we still need to control the number $D$ of $(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})$-excursions within the excursion $\widetilde X^1$
in order to apply (\ref{eq:geo-bd-ad}).  To this end,  
                  
note that to have $\{D \ge k\}$
                                                                      
                                    
requires at least $k$ visits from 
$\partial \Gamma_4 \subset \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},\tilde{r})$ to $\partial \Gamma_2$ before exiting 
$\mathbb{B}_{\mathsf{d}}({\bf 0},\tilde{R}) \subset \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d} (\mathsf{w},\rho_5):=\Gamma^\star_5$ where $\rho_5:=\tilde{R}+\tilde{r}$.
Similarly to our proof of (\ref{eq:st-dom}),  each of these $k \ge 1$ visits requires hitting 
$\partial \Gamma^\star_2$ before $\partial \Gamma^\star_5$ and the
probability of doing so is at most the maximum of the latter probability 
over starting points in $\partial \Gamma^\star_3 \subset \Gamma_4$,  which is 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:-J-par}
\gamma_3 := \frac{\log\Big(\frac{2\tilde{R}+2\tilde{r}}{2R-qR}\Big)}{\log\Big(\frac{2\tilde{R}+2\tilde{r}}{2r+qR}\Big)}
\le p_o \,,
\end{equation}
for some $p_o=p_o(a,b) < 1$ and all $q \le q_1$.  
                                                                
Consequently,  the number of $(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})$-excursions is stochastically dominated by $\mathsf {G}^o_{p_o}$,  
independent of the content of those excursions.  

Now,  for $\lambda>0$ and $3 c q e^{4 \lambda} \le 1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bd-psi}
\mathbb{E}\big[e^{4\lambda \mathsf {G}^o_{cq}}\big] = (1-c q) \sum_{k=0}^\infty (c q)^k e^{4 \lambda k} = 
\frac{1- c q}{1- c q e^{4 \lambda}} \le \exp\big(3 c q (e^{4\lambda}-1)\big)
\end{equation}
(as $e^{2t} (1-t)$ increase on $[0,\frac{1}{2}]$,   take here
$t=\frac{cq(e^{4\lambda}-1)}{1-cq}$).  Similarly,  setting $\psi_o:=\log(\frac{1+p_0}{2p_0})>0$
and $c_o:=\frac{1-p_0}{1+p_0}>0$,  we have that for any $\psi \in [0, \psi_o]$, 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bd-J-po}
\mathbb{E}[e^{\psi \mathsf {G}^o_{p_o}}] = \frac{1-p_0}{1-p_0 e^\psi} \le e^{\psi/c_o}\,.
\end{equation}
Further,  with $\log(1+t) \le t$,  we have for any $\lambda>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bd-psi-th}
\log \mathbb{E}\big[e^{4\pi \lambda \mathcal{B}_{c \sqrt{q}}}\big] + c \sqrt{q} \lambda 
                                                               
 \le 2 c \sqrt{q} (e^{4 \pi \lambda} - 1)\,.
\end{equation}
We thus deduce from (\ref{eq:bd-psi}) that for $\lambda>0$ with $e^{4 \lambda} \le \psi_o/(3 c q)$,
\[
\psi(\lambda) := \log \mathbb{E}\big[e^{4\lambda \mathsf {G}^o_{cq}}\big] \le 3 c q (e^{4 \lambda}-1) \le \psi_o \,,
\]
and likewise we have in view of (\ref{eq:bd-psi-th}) that when $e^{4\pi \lambda} \le \psi_o/(4 c \sqrt{q})$,
\[
\widetilde{\psi}(\lambda) := \psi(\lambda) + \log \mathbb{E}\Big[e^{4\pi \lambda \mathcal{B}_{c \sqrt{q}}}\Big] + c \sqrt{q} \lambda
\le 4 c \sqrt{q} (e^{4 \pi \lambda} - 1) \le \psi_o \,.
\]
Hence,  for such values of $\lambda$,  
 by (\ref{eq:st-dom})--(\ref{eq:st-dom-th}) and the strong Markov property of the Brownian path,  
\begin{align}\label{eq:pre-zav1}
\mathbb{E}^\mathsf{z}\big[\exp(\lambda |A_{\mathsf{x},1}-B_{\mathsf{y},1}|)\big] &\le \mathbb{E} \big[e^{\psi(\lambda) \mathsf {G}^o_{p_o}}\big] \le 
e^{\psi(\lambda)/c_o} \le e^{(3c/c_o) q (e^{4 \lambda}-1)} \,,\\
\mathbb{E}^\mathsf{z}\big[\exp(\lambda |A^\theta_{\mathsf{x},1}-B^\theta_{\mathsf{y},1}|)\big] &\le 
\mathbb{E} \big[ e^{\widetilde \psi(\lambda) \mathsf {G}^o_{p_o}} \big] \le e^{\widetilde \psi(\lambda)/c_o} \le e^{(4c/c_o) \sqrt{q} (e^{4 \pi \lambda} - 1)}
\label{eq:pre-zav1-th}
\end{align}
(utilizing on the {\sc\lowercase{rhs}} both (\ref{eq:bd-J-po}) 
and our bounds on $\psi(\lambda)$ and $\widetilde \psi(\lambda)$).

On the {\sc\lowercase{lhs}} of (\ref{eq:pre-zav1}) and (\ref{eq:pre-zav1-th}) we have the {\sc\lowercase{mgf}} of some variable $Y \ge 0$ measurable 
on the part of $\widetilde X^1$ inside $\mathbb{B}_{\mathsf{d}}({\bf 0},\tilde{r})$.
Similarly to \cite[(9.10)]{BRZ2},  
                                                                                                          
                                                                                                  
restricted to $\sigma(Y)$,  the Radon-Nikodym derivative $d\mathbb{P}^{\mathsf{z},\mathsf{v}}/d\mathbb{P}^{\mathsf{z}}$
due to conditioning on the end point of $\widetilde{X}^1$ is uniformly bounded by 
                                       
twice the maximum over $\mathsf{z}' \in \partial \mathbb{B}({\bf 0},\sqrt{\tilde r \tilde R})$ of the Poisson kernel 
$p(\mathsf{z}',\mathsf{v})$ for the exit measure of $\mathbb{B}({\bf 0},\tilde{R})$, 
divided by its minimum over such $\mathsf{z}'$.  With $c_1=c_1(a,b)>1$ the maximum value of this factor 
for $\tilde{r}/\tilde{R} \in [a,b]$,  we deduce that for any such $Y$ and $\lambda>0$,
\[
\mathbb{E}^{\mathsf{z},\mathsf{v}}[e^{\lambda Y}] \le 1 + c_1 (\mathbb{E}^{\mathsf{z}}[e^{\lambda Y}] -1) \le \Big(\mathbb{E}^{\mathsf{z}}[e^{\lambda Y}]\Big)^{c_1}
\] 
(with the {\sc\lowercase{rhs}} by the monotonicity in $x>0$ of $(e^{b x}-1)/x$,  when $b>0$).  Using this bound we absorb
the factor $c_1$ in the universal constant $c/c_o$ on the {\sc\lowercase{rhs}} of (\ref{eq:pre-zav1})-(\ref{eq:pre-zav1-th}),
                         
arriving at (\ref{eq-zav1}) and its analog for $|A^\theta_{\mathsf{x},1}-B^\theta_{\mathsf{y},1}|$.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:HigherMomentBound}
Denote by $\mathcal{H}^\star_\infty$ the $\sigma$-algebra of the Brownian motion excluding its
excursions $\{\widetilde X^{i},i \ge 1\}$ from $\partial \mathbb{B}_{\mathsf{d}}({\bf 0},\tilde{r})$ to
$\partial \mathbb{B}_{\mathsf{d}}({\bf 0},\tilde{R})$.  In the setting of \Cref{lem:HigherMomentBound},  for
any $N \ge 1$,  non-random $\{i_1,\ldots, i_N\}$ and $e^{4 \pi \lambda} \le 1/(q c_3)$,  a.s.
\begin{equation}
\label{basicexp-ad}
\mathbb{E} \Big( \exp(\lambda \sum_{\ell=1}^N |A_{\mathsf{x},i_\ell}-B_{\mathsf{y},i_\ell}|) \big| \mathcal{H}^\star_\infty \Big) 
\leq e^{c_3 q (e^{4 \pi \lambda}-1) N} \,.
\end{equation} 
Adjusting $c_3$, 
                                
one can bound the {\sc\lowercase{rhs}}
                       
for $\lambda \in [0,1]$ 
                                                     
by $e^{c_3 q \lambda N} \le (1+2 c_3 q \lambda)^N$ (reducing $q_1 \le 1/(2 c_3)$ if needed).
In particular,  for any $\varphi \ge 2 c_3 q N$,   a.s.
\begin{equation}\label{basicexp2}
                                                     
\mathbb{P} \Big(\sum_{\ell=1}^{N} |A_{\mathsf{x},i_\ell}-B_{\mathsf{y},i_\ell}| \ge \varphi \big| \mathcal{H}^\star_\infty \Big) 
\leq  e^{-\frac{1}{2} (\varphi \wedge N) }  \, .
\end{equation}
If conditionally on $\mathcal{H}^\star_\infty$,  the variables $\{\widetilde X^i\}$ are independent of a Geometric($p_2$) 
variable $\mathsf {G} \ge 1$,  then 
                                                    
for any $\lambda\in [0, \frac{p_{2}}{3}]$,
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E} \Big(\exp\big(\lambda\sum_{i=1}^{\mathsf {G}} |A_{\mathsf{x},i}-B_{\mathsf{y},i}|\big)\Big)\leq e^{\frac{4 c_{3}}{p_2} q \lambda} \, . 
\label{basicexp1}
\end{equation}
Upon adjusting $q$ as \Cref{lem:HigherMomentBound},  
the bounds (\ref{basicexp-ad})-(\ref{basicexp1}) apply for 
$|A^\theta_{\mathsf{x},i}-B^\theta_{\mathsf{y},i}|$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Conditioning on $\mathcal{H}^\star_\infty$ is equivalent to knowing the starting and ending points of 
our $N$ excursions,  making them thereby independent copies of the single excursion of 
\Cref{lem:HigherMomentBound}.  Thus,  (\ref{basicexp-ad}) is a direct 
consequence of (\ref{eq-zav1}).   
                                         
Using the simpler bound $e^{c_3 q N}$ at $\lambda=1$,  yields (\ref{basicexp2}) 
by Markov's inequality,  as $\varphi- c_3 q N \ge \frac{1}{2} (\varphi \wedge N)$ for any
$\varphi \ge 2 c_3 q N$.  Similarly,  using the conditional on $\mathcal{H}^\star_\infty$ 
independence between $\mathsf {G}$ and our excursions,  and summing 
the bound $(1+2 c_3 q \lambda)^{\mathsf {G}}$ in (\ref{basicexp-ad}) 
over the values of $\mathsf {G}$,  the {\sc\lowercase{lhs}} of (\ref{basicexp1}) is bounded by 
\[
p_2 \sum_{\ell=1}^\infty (1 + 2 c_3 q \lambda)^\ell (1-p_2)^{\ell-1} 
                                                               
\le \Big(1-\frac{2 c_3 q \lambda
        
}{p_2}\Big)^{-1} \le e^{\frac{4 c_{3}}{p_2} q \lambda} \,,
\]
provided $2 c_3 q \lambda \le p_2/3$.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- cns-1: body_md -->
\label{con:renew}
Let $\{I_i\}$ be {\sc\lowercase{iid}} Bernoulli($p_3$) variables,  independent of the Brownian 
excursions $\{\widetilde{X}^i\}$.  Starting at $J_0=1$ with initial measure $\mu$ for $\widetilde{X}^1$,  at 
               
the renewal times $J_j:=\inf\{i>J_{j-1}: I_i=1\}$ set the initial measure for $\widetilde{X}^{J_j}$ to be $\mu$
independently of $\{\widetilde{X}^i,  i < J_j\}$,  while each $\widetilde{X}^{i+1}$ with $I_{i+1}=0$ 
starts at the measure $\nu_{\mathsf{u}_{i}}$ for $\mathsf{u}_{i} := \widetilde{X}_\infty^{i} \in \partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},\tilde{R})$.
<!-- end cns-1 -->
<!-- lemma-40: body_md -->
\label{lem-equalmean}
Fixing $\mu$,  $p_3>0$ and $\{J_j\}$ as in Construction \ref{con:renew},  one has that:\\
(a).  For any $\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y} \in \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},\tilde{r}-R)$ and $j \ge 1$,  
\begin{align}
\mathbb{E}^\mu [ \bar V^\theta_j ] &= 0 \qquad
                                                                                 
                    
\hbox{and} \qquad
\mathbb{E}^\mu [\bar V_j ]  
 
=0
                                                                       
 \,.\label{4.2}
\end{align}
(b).  Further,  in case $\mu=\mu_{{\bf 0},\tilde{R}}^{\tilde{r}}$,  we have for any $\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y} \in \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},\tilde{r}-R)$ and
$i \ge 1$, 
\begin{align}
\mathbb{E}^\mu [ A^\theta_{\mathsf{x},i}-B^\theta_{\mathsf{y},i} | \{I_j\} ] &= 0 \qquad
\hbox{and} \qquad
\mathbb{E}^\mu [A_{\mathsf{x},i}-B_{\mathsf{y},i} | \{I_j\} ] =0
 \,.\label{4.2-cond}
\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-40 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
(a).  Our ergodic argument uses the Doeblin Markov chains of the starting points 
on $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},r)$ for the excursions to $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},R)$ and back,
the analogous chain for such excursions around $\mathsf{y}$ and the {\sc\lowercase{IID}} chain of $\mu$-distributed
starting points for blocks $[J_{j-1},J_j)$ of excursions 
from $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},\tilde{r})$ to $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},\tilde{R})$,  augmenting the state
of each chain with its excursion (block) length.\\
Since $\mathbb{T}^2$ and the Brownian semi-group of $X_\cdot$ are translation invariant,  setting 
\begin{equation}\label{dfn:D-th}
D_{\mathsf{x},k}:=\sum_{j=1}^{k} \cos(\theta_{j,\mathsf{x}})\,, \qquad 
D_{\mathsf{y},k}:=\sum_{j=1}^{k} \cos(\theta_{j,\mathsf{y}})\,,
\end{equation}
the function $\mathsf{u} \mapsto \mathbb{E}^{\mathsf{x}+\mathsf{u}}(D_{\mathsf{x},1})$ is independent of $\mathsf{x}$ 
and translating $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},\cdot)$ to $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{y},\cdot)$ 
by adding $\mathsf{y}-\mathsf{x}$,  maps the invariant measure $\mu_{\mathsf{x},r}^R$ into $\mu_{\mathsf{y},r}^R$.
Thus,  applying Birkhoff's ergodic theorem to the bounded (random) functional $\cos(\theta)$ 
and the chains of excursions around $\mathsf{x}$ and around $\mathsf{y}$,  we have that 
$k^{-1} D_{\mathsf{x},k}$ and $k^{-1} D_{\mathsf{y},k}$ converge a.s.  when 
$k \to \infty$,  to the same non-random limit (namely,  $\langle \cos(\cdot),\bar \mu \rangle$,  for $\bar \mu$ 
whose density is given in (\ref{dfn:Poiss})).  
Further,  with $N_\mathsf{x}(t)$ and $N_\mathsf{y}(t)$ counting the excursions completed by time $t$, 
from $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},r)$ to $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},R)$,  and from 
$\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{y},r)$ to $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{y},R)$,  respectively,  
the length of such excursions possess finite exponential moments,  
uniform in the corresponding starting points,  and by the Doeblin property 
of the underlying chain the consecutive excursion lengths form an (exponentially) mixing sequence.  
Thus,  applying Birkhoff's ergodic theorem for the average of the $\mathsf{x}$ and $\mathsf{y}$ excursion length,  
using again the translation invariance of $\mathbb{T}^2$ and $X_\cdot$,  we deduce that 
$t^{-1} N_{\mathsf{x}}(t)$ and $t^{-1} N_{\mathsf{y}}(t)$ have the same non-random limit when $t \to \infty$.  
It follows that 
\[
\frac{1}{t} \Delta_t:=\frac{1}{t} (D_{\mathsf{x},N_\mathsf{x}(t)}-D_{\mathsf{y},N_{\mathsf{y}(t)}}) =
\frac{D_{\mathsf{x},N_\mathsf{x}(t)}}{N_{\mathsf{x}}(t)}\frac{N_\mathsf{x}(t)}{t}-\frac{D_{\mathsf{y},N_{\mathsf{y}(t)}}}{N_{\mathsf{y}}(t)}\frac{N_{\mathsf{y}}(t)}{t}
\stackrel{a.s}{\to} 0 \,.
\] 
Next,  let  $T_j$ be the times of starting the $J_j$-th excursion from 
$\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},\tilde{r})$ to $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},\tilde{R})$
and $\widetilde N_{{\bf 0}}(t):=\sup\{j \ge 1:T_j \le t\}$.  Then,  by the renewal {\sc\lowercase{SLLN}} for the integrable 
time $T_2-T_1$, 
                                    
there exists non-random $\infty>b>0$,  such that for any $\delta>0$
                   
we have 
that $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{A}^{\complement}_{t,\delta}) \to 0$ for $\mathcal{A}_{t,\delta}:=\{|\widetilde N_{{\bf 0}}(t) - bt| \le \delta t-1\}$.  
                                                           
On  the event $\mathcal{A}_{t,\delta}$ we have 
that $t \in [T_{(b-\delta)t+1},T_{(b+\delta)t})$,  hence then  
\begin{equation}\label{eq:erg-ad}
|\Delta_{T_{bt}}| \le |\Delta_t| + \sum_{i = J_{(b-\delta) t}}^{J_{(b+\delta) t}-1} 
( A_{\mathsf{x},i}+ B_{\mathsf{y},i} )  
\end{equation}
(the last term counts the $\mathsf{x}$-excursions and $\mathsf{y}$-excursions in $[T_{(b-\delta)t},T_{(b+\delta)t})$).
With $\sup_{\mathsf{u}} \mathbb{E}^{\mathsf{u}} A_{\mathsf{x},1} + \sup_{\mathsf{u}'} \mathbb{E}^{\mathsf{u}'} B_{\mathsf{y},1} \le C$ and 
${\mathbf E} [J_j-J_{j-1}] = 1/p_3$,
by Markov's inequality the probability that the right-most term of (\ref{eq:erg-ad}) 
exceeds $2 \delta t \ell C/p_3$ is at most $1/\ell$.   Clearly,  
\[
\Delta_{T_{bt}}=\sum_{j=1}^{bt} \bar V^\theta_j \,,
\]
so dividing (\ref{eq:erg-ad}) by $b t$,  taking $t \to \infty$,  then $\delta \to 0$ followed by $\ell \to \infty$,  we
conclude that a.s.
\begin{equation}\label{eq:erg-ad2}
\lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{1}{bt} \sum_{i=1}^{bt} \bar V^\theta_j = 0 \,.
\end{equation}
By the {\sc\lowercase{SLLN}},  the limit in (\ref{eq:erg-ad2}) must match the corresponding mean 
$\mathbb{E}^\mu \bar V_j^\theta$,  yielding the {\sc\lowercase{lhs}} of (\ref{4.2}). \\ 
Now,   instead of (\ref{dfn:D-th}) set $D_{\mathsf{x},k}=D_{\mathsf{y},k}:=k$,  resulting with $\Delta_t = N_\mathsf{x}(t)-N_\mathsf{y}(t)$ 
and thereby with $\Delta_{T_{bt}} =\sum_{j \le bt} \bar V_j$.  Thus,  upon applying in this setting 
the same reasoning as above,  we arrive at the {\sc\lowercase{rhs}} of (\ref{4.2}).\\
(b).  Fixing $i \ge 1$,  the variables in (\ref{4.2-cond}) are measurable on $\widetilde X^i$,  hence their conditional 
expectations depend on $\{I_j\}$ only via the initial law of $\widetilde X^i$,  which in turn depends only on $\{I_j, j<i\}$.
Further,  as explained \cite[above (5.29)]{BRZ2},  in the invariant case $\mu=\mu_{{\bf 0},\tilde{R}}^{\tilde{r}}$,  
one has that $\mathbb{E}^\mu [ \nu_{\mathsf{u}_i} | \{I_j,j<i\} ] = \mu$,  so the conditional expectations 
in (\ref{4.2-cond}) are independent of $\{I_j\}$ and $i \ge 1$.  In particular,  then 
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}^\mu [\bar V^\theta_1] &= (\mathbb{E} J_1 -1)  \mathbb{E}^\mu [ A^\theta_{\mathsf{x},1}-B^\theta_{\mathsf{y},1} ] \,,\\
\mathbb{E}^\mu [\bar V_1] &= (\mathbb{E} J_1-1)  \mathbb{E}^\mu [ A_{\mathsf{x},1}-B_{\mathsf{y},1} ] \,,
\end{align*} 
with (\ref{4.2-cond}) an immediate consequence of (\ref{4.2}).
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- lemma-41: body_md -->
\label{lem:c3new}
For some $q_{1}, p_3>0$ and  $c_4<\infty$,  depending only on $a, b$,  
                          
and $\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y} \in \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d} ({\bf 0},\tilde{r}-R)$ with $q:=\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})/R \leq q_{1}$,  one  has that:\\
(a).  For $\mu=\mu_{{\bf 0},\tilde{R}}^{\tilde{r}}$ and $\bar V_j$ of (\ref{eq:def-barV}),
                                                                                    
                                                   
                               
\begin{align}\label{basicexp1-imp}
\mathbb{E}^\mu \Big[\exp\big(\lambda \sum_{j=1}^\ell \bar V_j \big)\Big] &\leq \exp\big(c_{4} q \lambda^2 \ell\big) \,,
\qquad \forall \ell \ge 1, \; |\lambda| \le \frac{p_3}{4}, \\
\label{eq-zav1-new}
\mathbb{E}^{\mu}\big[\exp(\lambda V_\ell) \big] &\le \exp\big(2 c_4 q \lambda^2 \ell\big)  \,, \qquad \forall \ell \ge 1,   \;
|\lambda| \le \frac{p_3}{8}\,.
\end{align}
Up to the adjustment of $q$ these bounds apply for $\sum_j \bar V^\theta_j$ and $V_\ell^\theta$,  respectively.\\
                                                                                                            
(b).   Further,  for any $\tilde{R}/\widehat R \in [a,b]$ and $\widehat R < \frac{1}{2}$,   
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}^{\mu_{{\bf 0},\tilde{R}}}\big[ \exp(\lambda V_\ell) \,\big| \, 
\ensuremath{T_{{\bf 0},\tilde{R}\to \tilde{r}}^{{\bf 0},\tilde{R}\overset{1}{\to}\widehat{R}} }
 = \ell \big] \leq \exp(2 c_4 q \lambda^{2} \ell)\,,
\quad \forall \ell \ge 1,  |\lambda| \le \frac{p_3}{8} 
\label{ergtotal.3}
\end{equation}
and the same applies for $V_\ell^\theta$,  upon adjusting $q$.
<!-- end lemma-41 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
By symmetry,  it suffices to consider $\lambda>0$ as we do hereafter. \\
(a).  By  the construction of our renewal times,  $\{\bar V_j\}$ are {\sc\lowercase{iid}} 
(and so are $\{\bar V_j^\theta\}$),  hence it suffices to establish  (\ref{basicexp1-imp})  for
 $\ell=1$.  In that case,  
from (\ref{basicexp1}) at $p_2=p_3$
and $\lambda=\frac{p_3}{3}$,  we deduce that for any $m \ge 1$, 
\[
\frac{(p_3/3)^m}{m!} \mathbb{E}\big( |\bar V_1|^m\big) \le \mathbb{E}\big( e^{\frac{p_3}{3} |\bar V_1|}\big) - 1 \le 
e^{\frac{4}{3} c_3 q}-1 \le \frac{8}{3} c_3 q \,.
\]
Hence,   in view of the {\sc\lowercase{rhs}} of (\ref{4.2}),  for $c_4:=96 c_3/p_3^{2}$ and $|\lambda| \le \frac{p_3}{4}$,  as claimed
\begin{equation}\label{basicexp1-imp-ad}
\mathbb{E} \big[e^{\lambda \bar V_1} \big] \le 1 + \sum_{m \ge 2} \frac{|\lambda|^m}{m!} \mathbb{E}\big( |\bar V_1|^m\big)
\le 1 + \frac{c_4}{4}
                          
 q  \lambda^2
\sum_{m \ge 0} \big(\frac{3}{4}\big)^m 
                       
\le e^{c_4 q \lambda^2} \,.
\end{equation}
Similarly,  combine (\ref{basicexp1}) for $\bar V_1^\theta$ with the {\sc\lowercase{lhs}} of (\ref{4.2})
to get (\ref{basicexp1-imp}) for $\bar V_1^\theta$.

Turning to  (\ref{eq-zav1-new}),  by Construction \ref{con:renew},  we have the renewals for 
$\mu=\mu^{\tilde{r}}_{{\bf 0},\tilde{R}}$ 
                                               
at random times $1=J_0 < J_1 < \cdots < J_{U_{\ell}} \le \ell$
                                                                                        
that break our excursions into $U_{\ell} < \ell$ segments,  each of $L_j:=J_j-J_{j-1}$ excursions, 
followed by a segment of $L_0:=\ell +1 -J_{U_{\ell}} \ge 1$ excursions.  
Conditioned on $\{J_j\}$ these segments are independent and therefore so are
$\bar V_0:=V_\ell-V_{J_{U_{\ell}}-1}$ and $\bar V_j := V_{J_j-1}-V_{J_{j-1}-1}$ for $1 \le j \le U_{\ell}$,
where by construction the conditional law of $\bar V_j$ depends only on the value of $L_j$.  
Further,  from the {\sc\lowercase{rhs}} of (\ref{4.2-cond}),  we deduce that 
$\mathbb{E}^\mu [\bar V_j | L_j ]=0$.  Thus,  by Jensen's inequality 
$\mathbb{E}^{\mu} [ e^{\lambda \bar V_j} | L_j ]  \ge 1$,  and thereby
\begin{align}
 \mathbb{E}^{\mu}\big[e^{\lambda V_\ell}\,\big
| \,  \{J_j\} \big] 
&=
\prod_{j=0}^{U_{\ell}} \mathbb{E}^{\mu} \big[ e^{\lambda \bar V_j} | L_j \big] \le 
                                                
 \prod_{j=0}^{\ell-1}  \mathbb{E}^{\mu} \big[ e^{\lambda \bar V_j} | L_j \big] \,.
\label{2renew.6ad}
\end{align}
Taking the expectation 
                                   
on both sides of (\ref{2renew.6ad}),  we deduce by 
Cauchy-Schwarz and the independence of $\{L_j,  j \ge 1\}$,  that 
\begin{align}
\Big( \mathbb{E}^{\mu}\big[e^{\lambda V_\ell}\,& \big]\Big)^2  
 \le  \mathbb{E} \Big(  \mathbb{E}^{\mu} \big[ e^{\lambda \bar V_0} | L_0 \big]^2 \Big) 
\mathbb{E} \Big( \prod_{j=1}^{\ell-1}  \mathbb{E}^{\mu} \big[ e^{\lambda \bar V_j} | L_j \big]^2 \Big) 
 \nonumber \\ & \le
\mathbb{E} \Big(  \mathbb{E}^{\mu} \big[ e^{2 \lambda \bar V_0} | L_0 \big] \Big) 
\mathbb{E} \Big( \prod_{j=1}^{\ell-1}  \mathbb{E}^{\mu} \big[ e^{2 \lambda \bar V_j} | L_j \big] \Big)  
 =  \prod_{j=0}^{\ell-1}  \mathbb{E}^{\mu} \big[ e^{2 \lambda \bar V_j} \big] 
\label{cs-Ls-ad}
\end{align}
By construction,  the  {\sc\lowercase{IID}} renewal epoch $\{L_j,  j\ge 1\}$ are positive
Geometric($p_3$),  so as in  (\ref{basicexp1-imp-ad}) we have that for any $j \ge 1$, 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bd-barVj}
\mathbb{E}^{\mu} \big[ e^{2 \lambda \bar V_j} \big] \le e^{4 c_4 q \lambda^2} \,,  \qquad \forall |\lambda| \le \frac{p_3}{8} \,.
\end{equation}
The {\sc\lowercase{rhs}} of (\ref{4.2-cond}) implies that ${\mathbf E}^\mu[\bar V_0|L_0] = 0$.  Further,  $L_0 \le \ell$,  
being the last passage epoch 
                 
before $\ell$,  
                              
is stochastically dominated by such positive Geometric($p_3$) variable.   
The derivation of (\ref{basicexp1-imp-ad}) thus applies for $\bar V_0$,
extending the validity of (\ref{eq:bd-barVj}) to all $j \ge 0$.  
Substituting this in (\ref{cs-Ls-ad}),  yields (\ref{eq-zav1-new}).

Using the {\sc\lowercase{lhs}} of (\ref{4.2-cond}) to deduce that $\mathbb{E}^\mu [\bar V^\theta_j | L_j ]=0$ for all $j \ge 0$, 
and adjusting $q$ to have (\ref{eq:bd-barVj}) holding for $\bar V^\theta_j$ instead of $\bar V_j$,  we get
by the same reasoning that (\ref{eq-zav1-new}) applies for $V^\theta_\ell$ instead of $V_\ell$.\\
(b).  In  (\ref{ergtotal.3}) we consider  
the sum of $\{A_{\mathsf{x},i}-B_{\mathsf{y},i}\}$ over the first $\ell$ excursions from $\mathsf{v}_i \in \partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},\tilde{r})$
to $\mathsf{u}_i \in \partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},\tilde{R})$ and back,  conditioned to stay inside $\mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},\widehat R)$.
Just like $\widetilde{X}^i$ of \cite[Section 5]{BRZ2},  these
are excursions of a \emph{planar Brownian motion} between concentric balls,  which here 
are further conditioned to remain inside a larger,  concentric ball.  Note that 
the Markov chain 
                    
$\{\mathsf{u}_i,  i \le \ell\}$,  whose (uniform) invariant measure $\mu_{{\bf 0},\tilde{R}}$ 
induces starting the $\partial \mathbb{B}_{\mathsf{d}}({\bf 0},\tilde{r})$-valued chain $\{\mathsf{v}_i\}$ 
at its invariant measure $\mu_{{\bf 0},\tilde{r}}$,  is independent of 
$\{T:=\ensuremath{T_{{\bf 0},\tilde{R}\to \tilde{r}}^{{\bf 0},\tilde{R}\overset{1}{\to}\widehat{R}} }=\ell\}$ (ie,
first hitting $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},\widehat R)$ just before the inner part 
of the $(\ell+1)$'st excursion).  Thanks to our assumptions on $\widehat R$,  $\tilde{R}$ and $\tilde{r}$,
the Brownian hitting measure of  $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},\tilde{r})$ 
\emph{conditioned to stay inside $\mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},\widehat R)$},  which 
with some abuse of notation we now denote also as $\mathbb{P}^\mathsf{u}$,  satisfies
(\ref{eq:unif-p3}).  This allows us to apply the procedure of Construction \ref{con:renew}
now with $p_3=p_3(a,b)$ and $\mu:=\mu_{{\bf 0},\tilde{r}}$,  to get renewal times 
$1=J_0 < J_1 < \cdots < J_{U_{\ell}} \le \ell$ for the starting points $\{\mathsf{v}_i\}$ of the 
excursions $\widetilde X^i$ which are now further conditioned to stay inside $\mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},\widehat R)$.
As before,  the renewal times break our excursions into $U_{\ell} < \ell$ segments,  each  
of $L_j$ excursions that are conditioned to stay inside $\mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},\widehat R)$,  
followed by a segment of $L_0 \ge 1$ excursions,  at the end of which the Brownian 
path reaches $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},\widehat R)$.  Conditioned on $\{J_j\}$ and $\{T=\ell\}$,  
these segments are independent,  resulting with $\bar V_j$,  $0 \le j \le U_{\ell}$ being
conditionally mutually independent,  with the conditional law of $\bar V_j$ depending only on the value of $L_j$.
Starting at $\mu$ which is also the invariant measure of the chain $\{\mathsf{v}_i\}$ we further deduce,
as in the derivation of (\ref{4.2-cond}) that  for $1 \le i \le \ell$, 
\begin{equation*}
               
\mathbb{E}^\mu [ A^\theta_{\mathsf{x},i}-B^\theta_{\mathsf{y},i} \,|\,  \{I_j\},  T=\ell ] = 0 \quad
\hbox{and} \quad
\mathbb{E}^\mu [A_{\mathsf{x},i}-B_{\mathsf{y},i} \,|\, \{I_j\}, T =\ell ] =0\,.
\end{equation*}
Therefore,  as in part (a),  here too $\mathbb{E}^\mu [\bar V^\theta_j | L_j ]=0$ and $\mathbb{E}^\mu[\bar V_j | L_j]=0$.
Proceeding hereafter as in the proof of (\ref{eq-zav1-new}),   but with extra conditioning on $\{T=\ell\}$ 
and using now $\mu=\mu_{{\bf 0},\tilde{r}}$,  we thus get similarly to (\ref{2renew.6ad}) that 
\begin{align}
 \mathbb{E}^{\mu}\big[e^{\lambda V_\ell}\,\big
| \, T = \ell ,  \{J_j\} \big] 
&=
\prod_{j=0}^{U_{\ell}} \mathbb{E}^{\mu} \big[ e^{\lambda \bar V_j} | L_j \big] \le 
                                                
 \prod_{j=0}^{\ell-1}  \mathbb{E}^{\mu} \big[ e^{\lambda \bar V_j} | L_j \big] \,.
\label{2renew.6}
\end{align}
Take the expectation with respect to $\{J_j,j \ge 1\}$ on both sides of (\ref{2renew.6}),  to 
likewise arrive by Cauchy-Schwarz and the independence of $\{L_j,  j \ge 1\}$,  at
\begin{align*}
\Big( \mathbb{E}^{\mu}\big[e^{\lambda V_\ell}\,& \big| \, T = \ell \big]\Big)^2  
                                                                       
                                                                                       
           
\le
                                                                 
                                                                                          
  \prod_{j=0}^{\ell-1}  \mathbb{E}^{\mu} \big[ e^{2 \lambda \bar V_j} \big] \,.
              
\end{align*}
As before,   (\ref{eq:bd-barVj}) holds for $0 \le j < \ell$,  thereby resulting with 
(\ref{ergtotal.3}) and upon adjusting $q$ as usual,  the same argument applies also for $V^\theta_\ell$.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- lemma-42: body_md -->
\label{lem-cont1}
For any $C_{0}<\infty$ there exist $c_1<\infty$,  $c_{0},   q_{0} >0$,  depending only on $a,b,C_0$,
so for any $n \ge 1$ and 
$\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y} \in \mathbb{B}_{\mathsf{d}}({\bf 0},\widetilde{r}-R)$ with $q:=\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})/R\leq q_{0}$,
\begin{align}
\mathbb{P}\left(\left| \ensuremath{T_{\mathsf{x},R\to r}^{{\bf 0},\tilde r\overset{n}{\to}\tilde R} }
        - \ensuremath{T_{\mathsf{y},R\to r}^{{\bf 0},\tilde r\overset{n}{\to}\tilde R} }
        \right|\ge\theta\sqrt{  qn}
\right) & \le  e^{-C_{0}\theta^{2}\sqrt{q}}\quad  \forall \theta \in [c_1, c_{0}\sqrt{n}\,] \,,
\label{cb.1} \\
\mathbb{P}\left(\left| \ensuremath{T_{\mathsf{x},R\to r}^{{\bf 0},\tilde r\overset{n}{\to}\tilde R} }
        - \ensuremath{T_{\mathsf{y},R\to r}^{{\bf 0},\tilde r\overset{n}{\to}\tilde R} }
        \right|\ge\theta\sqrt{  qn}
\right)
& \le e^{-C_{0}\theta} \,, \qquad 
\forall \theta \in [c_{1}, (nq)^{2} \wedge c_0 n] \,. 
\label{cb2.0}
\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-42 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
In view of (\ref{1.5tot}),  this is about tail estimates for $V_n$ of (\ref{eq:def-V}) and the proof of
(\ref{cb.1}) parallels that of \cite[(5.7)]{BRZ2}, 
                                                                                                      
                                                  
                                         
                 
                                                                                                                                                         
     
                                                      
except that here we do not condition on their events $Y_m \in \mathcal{I}_m$.
Indeed,  we merely follow the bound of  \cite[(5.35)-(5.36)]{BRZ2},  utilizing in \cite[(5.37)]{BRZ2}
our bound (\ref{basicexp1-imp}) for their ``main" term $A_1$,  while using 
(\ref{basicexp1}) to control the ``reminder'' term $A_2$ there.
      
                 
                                                                      
                                                                                           
Armed with the above,  the reader can check that the proof of \cite[(5.7)]{BRZ2} carries over 
here to get (\ref{cb.1}).  

Turning to larger values of $\theta$ (that exhibit
the transition from Gaussian moderate deviations to exponential large deviations),  the 
proof of (\ref{cb2.0}) proceeds similarly,  by adapting \cite[proof of Lemma 5.6]{BRZ2}.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- lemma-43: body_md -->
\label{lem-cont3}  
For any $C_{0}<\infty$ there exist  $c_1<\infty$,  $q_0>0$,  depending only on $a,b,C_0$,
so if  (\ref{eq-ratiobounds}) holds for $\tilde{r}= r_{k'}$ and $\tilde{R}=r_{k'-1}$,  then for 
any $n \ge 1$ and $\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y} \in \mathbb{B}_{\mathsf{d}}({\bf 0},\widetilde{r}-R)$ with $q:=\mathsf{d}(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{y})/R\in [\frac{c_1^2}{n}, q_{0}]$,
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{P}\Big(
\big| \ensuremath{T_{\mathsf{x},R\to r}^{{\bf 0},r_{k'}\overset{n}{\to} r_{k'-1}} }
        - \ensuremath{T_{\mathsf{y},R\to r}^{{\bf 0},r_{k'}\overset{n}{\to}r_{k'-1}} }
        \big|
\ge\theta\sqrt{  qn}\,\Big| 
\, T_{k'}^{{\bf 0},\bar k,m} = n, \, {\mathcal G}_{\bar k}^{\bf 0} \Big)
 \le e^{-C_{0}\theta}\,,
\label{cb2.1}
\end{equation}
for all $\theta \ge c_{1}$,  $m \ge 1$ and $k' - \bar k \ge 2 \vee \log (n \log n)$.
<!-- end lemma-43 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
We will show for some 
$p_4,q_0>0$,  $c_5, C<\infty$ depending only on $a$,  $b$,
\begin{eqnarray}
 \mathbb{E}\big(e^{\lambda V_n} 
 \,\big| \, 
T_{k'}^{{\bf 0},\bar k,m} = n, \, {\mathcal G}_{\bar k}^{\bf 0} \big)\leq C e^{ c_5 q  \lambda^{2} n}, 
\quad \forall n \ge 1,  \lambda \in [0,p_4]\,,  q \le q_0 \,.
\label{ergtotal.1}
\end{eqnarray}
By Chebyshev's inequality,  such a bound implies that
\begin{align}\label{2renew3a}
\mathbb{P}\big( V_n \ge\theta\sqrt{q n}\,\Big
| \, T_{k'}^{{\bf 0},\bar k,m}
 = n, \, {\mathcal G}_{\bar k}^{\bf 0} \big) 
& \leq  C e^{ c_5 q  \lambda^{2} n} e^{ -\lambda \theta\sqrt{qn}}.
\end{align}
By symmetry,  (\ref{2renew3a}) holds also for $-V_n$.   Recalling (\ref{1.5tot}) and taking 
$\lambda = \min\{ \theta/(2c_5\sqrt{qn}), p_4\}$,  we bound the 
logarithm of the {\sc\lowercase{lhs}} of (\ref{cb2.1}) by
\[
\log (2C) - \frac{\theta}{4c_5} \min\{\theta, 2 p_4 c_5 \sqrt{qn}\}  \le - C_0 \theta \,,
\]
provided $\theta \wedge \sqrt{qn} \geq c_1$, 
with $c_1$ large enough (depending on $p_4$,  $c_5$,  $C$ and $C_0$). 

Turning to prove (\ref{ergtotal.1}),  let $Z_{k'}^{i'}$ count the excursions from $\partial \mathbb{B}_{\mathsf{d}}({\bf 0},r_{k'-1})$ to $\partial \mathbb{B}_{\mathsf{d}}({\bf 0},r_{k'})$ during the $i'$'th excursion from $\partial \mathbb{B}_{\mathsf{d}}({\bf 0},r_{\bar k})$ to $\partial \mathbb{B}_{\mathsf{d}}({\bf 0},r_{\bar k-1})$ and set 
\[
C := \sup_{\ell \ge 2 \vee \log (n\log n)} \{ (1+ 28.2 (\ell+1) e^{-\ell})^n \} < \infty \,.
\]
By the law of total probability,  (\ref{ergtotal.1}) follows upon showing for 
$s_m := \displaystyle{\sum_{j=1}^m} \ell_{j}$,  $S :=1+ 28.2 (k'-\bar k+1) e^{-(k'-\bar k)}$
and any fixed $\{ \ell_{j} \in \mathbb{Z}_+,  j \ge 1\}$, 
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}\big( e^{\lambda V_{s_m}} \,\big
| \, \{Z^{i'}_{k'}=\ell_{i'}, i'\le m\} , \, {\mathcal G}_{\bar k}^{{\bf 0}} \big)\leq (S e^{  c_5 q \lambda^{2}})^{s_m} 
\,,\quad \forall \lambda\in (0,p_4]\,,
\label{ergtotal.1z}
\end{equation}
Setting $V_0:=0$  and
                                                                                      
$T := \ensuremath{T_{{\bf 0},r_{k'-1}\to r_{k'}}^{{\bf 0},r_{k'-1}\overset{1}{\to}r_{\bar k-1}} }$ counting
the $k'$-level excursions around ${\bf 0}$ till reaching $\partial \mathbb{B}_\mathsf{d}({\bf 0},r_{\bar k-1})$,  note that 
by \cite[(9.7)]{BRZ2}
\begin{align}
 \mathbb{E}\big(e^{\lambda V_{s_m}} \,\big|  \, \{Z^{i'}_{k'}=\ell_{i'}\} ,  \, {\mathcal G}_{\bar k}^{{\bf 0}} \big)
& =\mathbb{E}\big(\prod_{j=1}^{m} e^{\lambda (V_{s_j}-V_{s_{j-1}})}
\,\big| \, \{Z^{i'}_{k'}=\ell_{i'}\} , \, {\mathcal G}_{\bar k}^{{\bf 0}} \big) 
\nonumber \\ & 
\leq \prod_{j=1}^{ m} \, S^{\ell_{j}} \,
\mathbb{E}^{\mu_{{\bf 0},r_{k'-1}}} \big(e^{\lambda V_{\ell_{j}}}\,\big| T = \ell_{j}\big).
 \label{2renew.4}
\end{align}
Thus,  applying (\ref{ergtotal.3}) for
$\tilde{r}=r_{k'}$,  $\tilde{R}=r_{k'-1}$,  $\bar R = r_{\bar k-1}$ and $\ell=\ell_{j}$ for $1 \le j \le m$,  
yields (\ref{ergtotal.1z}),  thereby completing the proof of the lemma.
